questions.q: In the capstone scenario (50 logical qubits at code distance 21), what is the physical-qubit cost per logical qubit, and how is it computed?
options: 50, equal to the number of logical qubits
21, equal to the code distance itself
questions.explain: Using the verified surface-code formula total=2d^2-1 with d=21: 2(441)-1=881 physical qubits per logical qubit.

questions.q: What is the total physical-qubit cost (for the base error-correcting code alone) for 50 logical qubits at distance 21?
questions.explain: 50 x 881 = 44,050, the directly computed total before any additional magic-state distillation overhead.

questions.q: Why does the capstone note that 44,050 is the cost 'before adding magic-state distillation overhead'?
options: Because distillation (chapter 7) adds a separate, additional layer of physical qubits and operations on top of the base QEC cost, for any T gates the algorithm needs
Because magic-state distillation actually reduces the total qubit count below 44,050
Because distillation overhead was already included in the 2d^2-1 formula
Because the algorithm in this scenario uses no gates at all
questions.explain: The 2d^2-1 figure covers only the base surface-code protection; distillation (lesson 29) is a separate additional cost layered on top for universality.

questions.q: What role does the threshold condition (chapter 6) play in whether this 44,050-qubit system would actually achieve its intended protection?
options: The protection only materializes if the hardware's actual physical error rate is below the surface code's threshold p_th -- distance alone doesn't help otherwise
The threshold condition is irrelevant once a specific qubit count has been computed
The threshold theorem guarantees protection regardless of the physical error rate
Threshold only matters for the Steane code, not the surface code
questions.explain: As chapter 6 established, increasing distance only suppresses logical error rate exponentially if the physical error rate is below threshold -- a necessary precondition, not an automatic guarantee.

questions.q: What is the capstone's honest three-part conclusion about the current state of fault-tolerant quantum computing?
options: The theory (threshold theorem) says scaling up is worth it, the arithmetic says exactly what it costs, and current NISQ-era hardware isn't yet at the scale required -- all three true simultaneously
Fault-tolerant quantum computing has already been fully achieved at this scale
The threshold theorem has been proven false, so scaling up never helps
Resource estimation arithmetic is purely theoretical and has no bearing on real hardware
questions.explain: The capstone's explicit synthesis holds all three facts together -- favorable theory, large but computable real cost, and an honest current-hardware gap -- rather than collapsing into either false optimism or false pessimism.
